The suitors looked at one another across the hall. Their voices dropped to a murmur, and they glanced often toward the door where the stranger had stood.

Telemachus kept his face calm. He picked up his cup and drank slowly, as if nothing at all troubled him. He said little more about Mentes or his father.

Eurymachus leaned close to his friends and whispered something. Antinous laughed under his breath, but his eyes kept sliding back to Telemachus. They could tell that he was hiding something, yet they could not guess what it was.

The feast went on. Singers plucked their lyres, and the wine jars were filled again and again. Slowly the whispering faded into yawns and tired jokes.

Telemachus rose quietly and slipped out of the hall while the men were busy with their cups. Nobody stopped him. As the sun sank and the shadows grew long, the suitors stretched and stood up. One by one they wandered off to their own homes to rest, ready for the story to go on.

text:
Telemachus waited until the hall grew quiet. Then he slipped past the great gate and out into the cool night air.

He walked quickly down the path toward the harbour. The stranger had spoken of a ship waiting there, and he wanted to see it with his own eyes.

The sea lay calm and silver under the moon. Small waves touched the stones without a sound. Telemachus looked along the shore, but no ship rode at anchor.

Only a single gull sat on a rock, watching him with bright eyes. It rose and drifted away over the water.

Telemachus thought about the words the stranger had spoken. Minerva had told him to seek news of his father, and to go out into the wide world to find him. Had she truly been a stranger at all?

He understood then that the ship had already gone. Whoever had come to his house was far away by now.

He turned and walked back quietly. He slipped through the gate again and crossed the empty hall, keeping close to the shadows so no suitor would notice him.

The fires had burned low. The night grew late, and the house fell silent around him.

Telemachus climbed the stairs slowly, thinking hard about all that he had heard.

text:
Telemachus raised his hand and caught the eye of Phemius, the bard, who sat near the hearth with his lyre across his knees. The young prince called him over with a quiet nod.

“Do you remember Mentes, the chief of the Taphians?” Telemachus asked in a low voice. “He was an old friend of my father’s.”

Phemius lifted his shoulders and let them fall. “I sing of heroes and of the long wars at Troy, my prince. I know nothing of ships or of the men who sail them.”

He bent his head over his lyre and began to pluck the strings again. The notes rose softly above the noise of the hall, then grew quieter still.

Telemachus thanked him with a kind word and got to his feet. The feast was still going on around him, and the suitors laughed loudly over their wine.

He did not stay to watch them. He walked slowly out of the hall, past the tables and the servants clearing away the cups. Outside, the air was cool, and the sky had grown dark.

The night’s quiet settled over the house. Somewhere a dog barked once and then fell silent. Telemachus climbed the stairs, still thinking about the stranger who had vanished so quickly from the hall.

prompt: The suitors are curious about the stranger who vanished. What should Telemachus do before bedtime?

text:
Telemachus said nothing about the goddess. He kept her secret close, like a stone held in his fist. Instead, he looked carefully at the men around him.

Eurymachus laughed loudly and spoke too quickly, as if he wanted everyone to listen. Antinous drank cup after cup of wine and never seemed to stop eating. Telemachus counted the bread and meat that vanished from the table.

Another suitor kept whispering behind his hand to the man beside him. Their eyes kept sliding toward the great doors, as if they feared someone might walk through them. Telemachus marked every glance and every whisper.

He tucked these things away in his mind. Tomorrow he would call the assembly, as he had promised. He would need to speak clearly and show the men of Ithaca what was being done in his house.

The feast slowly came to an end. Servants cleared the tables, and the singers put away their harps. The suitors stretched, yawned, and talked in low voices of their own affairs.

Telemachus felt tired, but his thoughts would not rest. Minerva’s words still rang in his ears. He had been told to be brave, and he meant to try.

At last he rose from his seat. He nodded politely to the older guests, then walked slowly toward the stairs. His heart was heavy, yet a small spark of hope burned inside him.

prompt: The suitors are curious about the stranger who vanished. What should Telemachus do before bedtime?
optionLabel: Tell the suitors plainly that the stranger was a god
brief: Telemachus stands and announces to the hall that the visitor was a goddess in disguise. The suitors laugh, then grow uneasy as the room falls silent. text:
Telemachus felt his heart beat hard. He set down his cup and stood up from his seat. The whole hall turned to look at him.

“Eurymachus, and all you suitors,” he said in a clear voice, “the stranger was no man. He was a goddess, Minerva, who came to me in the shape of Mentes.”

For a moment nobody spoke. Then a loud laugh rose from one of the young men near the door, and others joined in. Some of them shook their heads and smiled, as if he had made a joke.

But the laughter died away slowly. The suitors looked at one another. Their faces grew uneasy, and they began to shift on their benches. No one wanted to be the first to speak.

Telemachus felt braver than he had ever felt in that hall. Yet a cold worry crept into his chest. He wondered what these men might do to him once the night was dark.

He sat back down slowly. After a while, the feasting started again, but the voices were quieter now. Telemachus kept his eyes on his plate and thought of his father far away.

When the meal was over, he rose and climbed the stairs toward his room. He did not look back at the hall.

prompt: Telemachus prays alone by the grey sea, and the goddess Minerva is near. What should he do next?
optionLabel: Wait by the shore for a sign
brief: Telemachus sits on the rocks as the waves roll in. A gull lands near him and seems to watch him closely. Soon a stranger in Mentor's shape walks up, speaks kindly, and promises that a good ship will be found. Telemachus thanks him and turns homeward, troubled but hopeful.
text:
Telemachus stood alone on the rocks above the sea. The waves rolled in, grey and cold, and broke white against the stones at his feet. He had prayed hard, and now he waited to see what would come.

A gull came down over the water and landed on a flat rock close by. It turned its head and looked at him with bright, steady eyes. Telemachus found he could not look away from it. He felt that it was watching him with a purpose.

Then a man came walking along the shore. His step was calm and his beard was grey. Telemachus knew the shape of him at once, for it was Mentor, his father’s old friend.

“Do not be afraid, Telemachus,” the man said kindly. “You have asked for help, and help is near. Your father was a brave man, and you have shown courage today. A good ship will be found for you, and you will not sail alone.”

Telemachus rose and thanked him with a full heart. Still, he was troubled by many thoughts. The suitors were strong, and his house was full of their noise.

He turned his face toward home. The gull lifted from its rock and flew out over the waves. Telemachus walked on up the path, hopeful but uneasy, and he did not look back again.

The road ahead was long, and he knew it. Yet for the first time in many days, he felt that he was not alone.

prompt: Telemachus prays alone by the grey sea, and the goddess Minerva is near. What should he do next?
optionLabel: Ask the fishermen on the beach for help
brief: Telemachus walks along the sand and finds fishermen mending their nets. They quietly say the suitors are strong, but a few men might still row for the son of Ulysses. They tell him the best ships are kept in the harbour. He thanks them and sets off homeward with new courage.
text:
Telemachus walked slowly along the sand, away from the crowd and the grey waves. His heart still beat fast from the goddess’s words. He did not yet know what to do next.

At the far end of the beach, he saw a group of fishermen mending their nets. They sat on upturned boats, their hands moving quickly over the cords. Telemachus went closer and greeted them politely.

The oldest fisherman looked up and studied his face. He spoke quietly, so that no one on the road could hear. “The suitors are strong, young lord, and they are many. Anyone who stands against them must be very careful.”

Another man leaned forward. “But a few brave men might still row for the son of Ulysses. We remember your father with honour.”

They told him the best ships were kept in the harbour, beside the old stone quay. Telemachus thanked them with warmth and gave them his full attention. He felt his courage grow stronger with every word.

He turned back up the beach. The wind pushed at his cloak, and the gulls cried overhead. Telemachus set off homeward with a lighter step, ready to think about the voyage ahead.

text:
Telemachus did not wait by the sea any longer. He turned from the grey waves and walked quickly back toward the town of Ithaca.

The road was dusty, and the sun was hot on his shoulders. He passed the sheep pens near the edge of the fields, where the shepherds were already busy with their flocks.

His mind was full of thoughts. He kept thinking about the long journey to Pylos and to Sparta. Would he find King Nestor there? Would he hear any true news of his father?

He told himself that he must be brave. He also told himself he must be careful, and wise in all that he did. A foolish boy would not return from such a voyage.

He thought of the wine jars and the barley meal that he must have stored for the trip. There was much to prepare, and not much time.

By the time he reached the gates of his father’s house, his heart was steady. He straightened his back and lifted his chin. He was ready now to face the suitors, whatever they might say.

prompt: Telemachus prays alone by the grey sea, and the goddess Minerva is near. What should he do next?

brief: Telemachus kneels on the wet stones and prays once more, asking for a clear sign. The wind drops and he hears gulls calling over the bay. He feels calmer and resolves to sail to Pylos. He walks back toward the town, ready to face the suitors.
text:
Telemachus knelt on the wet stones at the edge of the sea. The spray cooled his face, and he felt small beside the great grey waves.

He lifted his hands and prayed again, more slowly this time. “Goddess, I need a clear sign,” he said. “Show me that you hear me, and that my father is still alive.”

For a moment nothing happened. Then the wind dropped, and the waves grew quiet. Over the bay, gulls began to call to one another.

Telemachus listened closely. Their cries rose and fell, bright and steady, and his heart slowed. He no longer felt so alone.

He thought of his father, lost for so many years, and of the long road that might lead to news of him. He would sail to Pylos, and perhaps to Sparta after that. He would not let fear turn him back.

He stood up and dried his hands on his cloak. The sea still shone behind him, calm and pale.

Then he turned and walked back up the path toward the town. His steps were firm now. The suitors were waiting in his father’s house, and he was ready to face them.

Telemachus stood by the grey water and listened to the waves hiss against the stones. His prayer had left him feeling small, yet also a little braver than before.

He walked slowly along the harbour road. Fishing boats rocked beside the wooden posts, and their ropes creaked in the wind. Some of the ships were old, with cracked planks and faded paint. Others looked newer and better cared for.

Then he saw one ship that stood out from the rest. Her hull was sturdy, and her sail was strong and well folded. He wondered whose ship she was, and whether her owner would lend her to a boy like him.

He glanced back toward the town. He thought of the suitors, loud and careless in his father’s hall. Would they try to stop him if they heard of his plan? The thought made his stomach tighten.

He did not stay long. Telemachus turned away from the harbour and climbed the path toward home. He had supplies to gather, and he would need every hour.

When he reached the house, the sound of laughter floated out through the doors. The suitors were still feasting, as they always did. Telemachus took a deep breath and walked toward them.

Then a white gull landed on a rock nearby. It folded its wings and turned its head to look at him. It did not fly away, and it seemed to watch him very closely.

Telemachus felt a strange calm settle over him. He thought of his father, who had been gone so many years. Was this a sign that the gods were listening?

Soon a man came walking along the shore. He wore the shape of Mentor, the old friend of his father, and his voice was warm and kind.

“Do not be afraid, Telemachus,” the stranger said. “If you are brave like your father, your voyage will not fail. I will find you a good ship, and I will sail with you myself.”

Telemachus rose and bowed his head. “Thank you,” he said. “I will do as you say.”

He turned and walked slowly back toward home. His thoughts were troubled, but a small hope burned inside him. The gull rose into the air and flew out over the grey sea.

prompt: Telemachus prays alone by the grey sea, and the goddess Minerva is near. What should he do next?

brief: Minerva steps out from the shore grasses in Mentor's form. She praises Telemachus for his courage and says his father would be proud. She promises to find a good ship and to sail with him. Then she sends him home to gather supplies before the suitors wake.
text:
Minerva stood still for a moment, watching the prince kneel by the grey water. Then she stepped out from the tall grass on the shore. She took the shape of Mentor, the old friend of Ulysses, and her voice was warm and steady.

“Telemachus,” she said, “you have spoken well today. Your courage pleases me more than you know. Your father would be proud to see you stand up in the assembly and speak against the suitors.”

Telemachus turned, surprised, and his face grew bright. He had not expected to find a friend on the lonely shore.

Minerva smiled, for she knew more than she said. “Do not fear the voyage. I will find a good ship for you, one that is strong and swift. I will sail at your side, and you will not go alone.”

She lifted one hand toward the town. “Now go home before the suitors wake. Gather food and wine for the road. Fill the jars and pack the barley meal in strong leather bags. Say nothing of your plans to anyone who might carry them to the suitors.”

The prince bowed his head. He felt his heart steady and his doubts grow quiet.

Minerva watched him walk up the path toward his father’s house. Then she turned away to find the ship and the crew that would carry them over the sea.

Telemachus raised his hands toward the grey water and called out to the goddess he could not yet see. He asked for help, for the wicked suitors were blocking every road he tried to take.

Then a figure stood close beside him on the wet sand. It wore the shape and the kind voice of Mentor, the old friend of his father. Minerva smiled behind that familiar face, for she knew more than she meant to say.

“Listen to me closely, Telemachus,” she said softly. “The suitors are plotting against you. They would be glad to see you lost at sea before you ever reach a far shore.”

Telemachus felt his heart beat faster. He looked back toward the house where the suitors were laughing and drinking.

“You must keep your plans secret,” Minerva went on. “Tell no one of your voyage except those you can trust. Trust me as well, for I will not leave you without help.”

She promised that a good ship would be ready and that she herself would sail with him. He would not face the sea alone.

“Go home now,” she urged. “Hurry, for there is no time to waste. Your journey must begin soon.”

Telemachus stood still for a moment, thinking of his father and of the long road ahead. Then he turned and began to walk back up the shore toward home.

The goddess watched him go with a steady, confident gaze.

Menelaus said nothing more. He saw that Telemachus needed time to gather himself, so he sat still and let the quiet fill the hall.

The guests murmured softly among themselves. Someone poured wine, and the room seemed to breathe slowly once again.

Then Helen came down from her high, vaulted room. She was perfumed and fair, and she looked as lovely as Diana herself. Her maids moved quickly to make her comfortable.

Adraste brought her a seat. Alcippe brought a soft woollen rug to cover her knees. Phylo fetched the silver work-box that Alcandra, the wife of Polybus, had given to Helen as a gift.

Polybus lived in Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the world. He had given Menelaus two silver baths, two tripods, and ten talents of gold. His wife had also given Helen fine presents, among them a golden distaff and a silver work-box on wheels, with a band of gold around its top.

Phylo set this box by Helen’s side. It was full of fine spun yarn. On top of it she laid a distaff wound with violet-coloured wool.

Helen took her seat and rested her feet on the footstool. Then she turned to her husband and was ready to ask her question.

Menelaus raised his hand and called to a servant. The man hurried off and soon returned with a silver basin of cool water. He poured it over Telemachus’s hands, and a clean towel was given to him.

Telemachus washed his face slowly. The cool water helped, and his heart grew a little lighter. He lowered his hands and looked up, a little embarrassed by his tears.

Menelaus smiled kindly at the young man. He said nothing more about the past, but his eyes showed that he understood.

Then a soft sound came from the stairs. Helen was coming down from her high room, which was vaulted and sweet with perfume. Her beauty was bright, like the goddess Diana’s.

Her maids moved quickly around her. One brought a chair, another carried a soft woollen rug, and a third fetched her silver work-box. The box was a gift that had been given to her long ago.

Helen sat down in the chair. She rested her feet on a small stool and spread the rug over her knees. Then she turned to her husband and began to ask about the strangers.

Telemachus stood up slowly, still holding his cloak. He did not want to speak, so he turned to Pisistratus and walked out into the courtyard.

The young men stood beside the chariot in the bright morning light. Its wheels gleamed, and its wood was polished smooth. Nearby, the horses stood sweating from the long road, but they looked well cared for. Grooms had already fed them with oats and barley, and they munched happily.

Telemachus put his hand on the neck of one horse. It was warm and strong. He thought of his father, who had also loved fine horses and fine ships.

Above them the sun shone on the palace walls. Gold and bronze caught the light and sparkled, so that the whole house seemed to glow. Pisistratus whistled softly at the sight.

Then the doors opened behind them. Helen came down from her high room, and her maids followed close behind her. They brought her a seat and set it in the sunlight. One maid laid a soft rug across it, and another brought a silver work-box filled with thread.

Helen settled herself in the seat with care. She rested her feet on the footstool and folded her hands. Telemachus and Pisistratus turned to face her, and the courtyard grew quiet as she prepared to speak.

Telemachus stood still with the cloak pressed to his face. For a long moment he could not speak. Then he slowly lowered the cloak and looked at the old king.

“Forgive me,” he said in a small voice. “I miss my father very much. I think of him every day, and I do not know where he is.”

His cheeks were wet, and he did not try to hide them now. He felt young and foolish, but he also felt that it was right to say it.

Menelaus looked at him with great kindness. He laid a warm hand on the young man’s shoulder and nodded slowly.

“There is no shame in tears, Telemachus,” he said gently. “Your father is a brave man, and I will help you find news of him. You have my word.”

Telemachus bowed his head. He felt a little steadier than before.

Then a soft rustle came from the stairs. Helen came down from her high room, as lovely as the goddess Diana. Her maids moved quickly around her. Adraste brought a seat, and Alcippe brought a soft woollen rug. Phylo carried the silver work-box that Alcandra had given her in Egypt.

Helen sat down with care. She rested her feet upon the footstool and arranged her skirts. Then she turned her bright eyes toward her husband, and she was ready to speak.

Telemachus felt his face grow hot. He leaned close to Pisistratus and whispered, so softly that only his friend could hear.

“What should I say to him? I do not want to speak foolishly in front of a king.”

Pisistratus did not laugh at him. Instead he squeezed Telemachus’s arm firmly, the way a brother might.

“Speak as my father Nestor taught us,” he whispered back. “Be honest, be respectful, and say what is in your heart.”

Telemachus remembered the old man’s kind voice and wise advice at Pylos. His shoulders loosened, and he sat up straighter. The knot of fear in his chest began to ease.

He lowered his cloak and looked at Menelaus. The king’s eyes were still kind, and they were patient.

Then a soft rustle sounded at the doorway. Helen came down from her high, sweet-smelling room, as lovely as the goddess Diana herself. Telemachus found it hard to look away from her.

Her maids moved quickly around her. Adraste brought a seat, and Alcippe spread a soft woollen rug over it. Phylo carried in a silver work-box, a gift from Alcandra, the wife of Polybus of Egyptian Thebes.

Helen settled into her seat with grace. She rested her feet on the footstool and gathered her thoughts. Then she turned to her husband, ready to ask about the guests.

Telemachus held his breath and waited for her words.

Menelaus said nothing more. He looked kindly at the young man and let the silence settle over the great hall.

Telemachus kept his cloak against his face. He breathed slowly and tried to steady himself. He was ashamed of his tears, but no one scolded him for them.

Around them the guests spoke softly to one another. Their voices were low, as if they knew a sad matter had come into the room. Pisistratus sat close beside him and said nothing at all.

Then a sweet scent drifted through the hall. Telemachus looked up, and his breath caught in his throat. Helen was coming down from her high, vaulted room. She looked as lovely as the goddess Diana.

Adraste hurried forward with a seat for her. Alcippe brought a soft woollen rug. Phylo carried in the silver work-box that Alcandra, the wife of Polybus, had given to Helen. It was full of fine spun yarn, and a distaff wrapped in violet wool lay across the top.

Helen sat down and rested her feet on the footstool. She folded her hands and looked at the young stranger with thoughtful eyes. Telemachus felt his heart beat faster. He wondered what she would say, and he waited to hear her voice.

text:
Ulysses pulled himself up from the mud and stood, shaking with cold. The sea still roared behind him, far off but never silent.

He turned and followed the river inland, keeping close to its bank. His feet slipped on wet stones, and his legs felt heavy as lead.

After a while he saw flat washing stones at the water’s edge. Beside them were footprints in the soft earth, small and neat, and he stopped to stare at them.

He listened hard. Somewhere in the distance he heard voices, faint and rising like birds calling at dusk. He called out, but no answer came.

He walked on until the light began to fail. The voices had faded, and he saw no house, no path, no fire.

Ulysses knew he could not search further tonight. His strength was gone, and the dark was coming fast.

He climbed the slope above the river, slowly and with great care. At the top stood a stand of trees, thick and dark against the sky.

He made his way toward them, where the wind could not reach him. There he would rest, and wait for morning to show him the way.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?

brief: Ulysses lies among the rushes and watches the calm river flow past. Fish flick in the shallows and a heron stands still nearby. A cold wind starts to blow off the water, so he gets up and climbs the bank toward the woods, keeping the sound of the river behind him.
text:
Ulysses did not sleep at once. He lay among the rushes and watched the river flow past him. The water was calm now, as smooth as glass, and it moved slowly toward the sea.

Small fish flicked in the shallows near the bank. Their silver backs caught the last light of the sun. A tall grey heron stood at the water’s edge, perfectly still, as if it were carved from stone.

Ulysses did not move for a long time. His arms ached, and his chest still burned from the salt water he had swallowed. He listened to the soft sound of the river and forgot, for a moment, the roar of the storm.

Then a cold wind began to blow off the water. It crept across the rushes and touched his wet skin. Ulysses shivered and knew he could not stay where he was.

He pushed himself up slowly. His legs felt heavy and weak. Step by step, he climbed the bank toward the dark line of trees on the higher ground.

He kept the sound of the river behind him. Each step took him farther from the water, and the evening grew colder around him.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?

brief: Ulysses closes his eyes for a short rest, then wakes to a bird calling in the trees. Looking up the slope, he spots a thick grove of olive trees whose branches grow so close they seem woven together. He decides it will keep off wind and rain, and he heads up the hill toward it.
text:
Ulysses lay still for a long while, his cheek pressed against the cold river bank. The rushes whispered around him, and the sea still roared far behind.

He meant only to rest for a moment. His eyes closed, and his tired body seemed to sink into the earth.

When he opened his eyes again, the sky had turned pale and grey. A bird was calling sharply from the trees above him. Its cry rang out again and again.

Ulysses raised his head slowly. His arms shook as he pushed himself up from the mud. Every bone in his body ached from the storm.

He looked up the slope toward the high ground. There, not far off, stood a thick grove of olive trees. Their branches grew so close together that they seemed woven into one another.

He thought that such a place would keep off the wind and the rain. It would be safer than the open river bed, where the night air was cold and damp.

So he gathered his strength and began to climb. Each step was hard, but he kept his eyes on the dark green leaves above him.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?

brief: Ulysses gathers his breath and calls out, but only the river answers. A dog barks somewhere far off, and he hears oars splashing beyond a bend. Too weak to go further, he takes this as a sign that people live nearby and that he must rest before searching. He crawls up the bank toward the trees.
text:
Ulysses lay still for a long while, listening. The river gurgled past him in the dark, and far behind the roar of the sea went on and on.

He gathered what breath he had left. Then he raised his head and called out, as loudly as his cracked voice would allow.

“Is anyone there? Hear me, if you are near!”

Only the river answered, with its soft and endless talk over the stones. Ulysses waited, his heart beating hard against his ribs.

Then, very far off, a dog barked. A moment later he heard the splash of oars beyond a bend in the river. Someone was out on the water, or not far from it.

Ulysses let out a slow breath. People lived here, then. That was good news, but he was too weak to go searching for them now. He must rest first, and find his strength again before he went looking.

He pulled himself up the bank on his elbows, one slow inch at a time. The mud was cold and the rushes scratched his face. Every movement cost him more than he had.

At last he reached higher ground, where the trees began. Their dark shapes rose above him against the fading sky. He set his eyes on them and kept crawling toward the shelter they offered.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?
optionLabel: Pray to the gods for courage and a place to rest
brief: Ulysses lifts his hands and asks the gods for help. A cool breeze rustles the reeds, and he feels a little stronger. He takes the wind as a sign to climb the slope, where thick trees may shelter him from the night air.
text:
Ulysses lay still on the cold bank and lifted his hands toward the sky. His arms shook, and his voice came out thin and rough from the salt water in his throat.

“Minerva, hear me,” he whispered. “You have watched over me before. Do not leave me now, in this strange land.”

He waited, and for a moment there was only the sound of the river and the distant roar of the sea. Then a cool breeze moved through the reeds. The tall stalks bent and rustled around him, and he felt the air touch his wet face.

Ulysses did not know whether the wind was a gift from the gods, but he chose to believe it was. He had learned long ago that a wise man reads every sign he is given. Slowly, he pushed himself up on one elbow.

He looked up the slope. Above him stood a thick growth of trees, dark against the last grey light of evening. Their branches looked close and full, the kind that could keep out the night air.

He was tired, cold, and hungry. Still, his legs felt a little stronger than before. Ulysses gathered his courage and began to climb toward the trees, one careful step at a time.

He followed the river inland, keeping the water on his left. The sound of the surf behind him slowly faded. In its place came the rustle of reeds and the cry of a bird far off.

Soon he came to flat stones beside the water, where people had clearly beaten their washing clean. Ulysses stopped and looked hard at them. Then he saw the marks of bare feet in the mud, and his heart beat faster. He stood very still and listened for voices.

For a while he heard only the river. Then, faint and distant, came the sound of people talking and laughing. Ulysses turned toward it, but the land rose steeply, and the light was going. He could not tell how far away the voices were.

He was too tired to search farther in the dark. Even a clever man could not walk far on legs like these. He thought of the cold wind that would come with the dawn, and of the wild beasts that roamed the hills at night.

So he decided to wait until morning. He climbed the slope with slow, careful steps, pulling himself up by the grass. At the top he saw a stand of trees, thick and dark against the sky. He made his way toward them, hoping to rest out of the wind.

He was alone, and he knew it. Still, he kept his thoughts steady, as he always did in hard times, and pressed on toward the trees.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?
optionLabel: Still the waves and hush the restless gulls
brief: Minerva calms the river's current and quiets the screaming gulls. The night air stays mild, so Ulysses can rest peacefully on the bank. Then she guides his tired steps up the slope toward a thick grove of olive trees, keeping the wind gentle.
text:
Minerva watched Ulysses lie still on the cold bank, his face pressed to the damp earth. Her grey eyes softened, though she would not let him see her there.

With a small motion of her hand, she called to the river. Its current slowed, and the brown water lay smooth as polished bronze. The waves that had raged behind him sank down and went quiet.

Overhead the gulls had been screaming and wheeling above the shore. Minerva hushed them with a word, and they settled on the sand like pebbles dropped from the sky.

The air grew mild and still. No chill crept off the water, and the night was kind to the weary man. Minerva knew the peace would not last forever. Neptune’s anger still burned far out on the deep sea, and his storm had only paused.

She stepped close to Ulysses and touched his shoulder lightly. He stirred, groaning, and lifted his head with great effort.

“Rise, Ulysses,” she said softly. “The land is kind to you tonight. Climb the slope, where the trees grow thick.”

He rose on trembling legs and climbed, one slow step after another. Minerva kept the wind gentle around him, so no cold breath could follow him up the hill. Above him stood a grove of olive trees, dark and close together, waiting for him.

prompt: Ulysses lies cold and alone on the riverbank, the sea still roaring behind him. What should he do before night falls?

Minerva watched from the high places of heaven as Ulysses lay among the rushes. His face was pale, and his limbs shook with cold. She could not bear to see him so weak.

She did not show herself. Gods who wish to help a mortal must often do it in silence, and she knew it was better so. Instead she sent a quiet thought into his tired mind.

The high ground above the river, she whispered, held a thick grove of trees. Its branches were close and strong, and they would keep out the wind and the damp.

Ulysses stirred. He lifted his head and looked about him, as though he had heard a voice he could not quite name. Then he drew a slow breath, and his shivering eased a little.

“Something tells me I should climb,” he murmured, and he rose stiffly to his feet.

Minerva followed him with her eyes as he began the climb. She kept close watch over every step he took. Where the ground was steep, she made the stones sit firm beneath his feet. Where the path ran through brambles, she turned them aside.

The wind stayed soft as he climbed. The sea below grew quieter, as if it too wished him no harm.

Minerva smiled to herself. Ulysses would find his shelter, and he would never know who had guided him there.

Minerva followed him with her eyes. She was pleased, and she waited to see what he would do next.

Ulysses parted the leaves of his bush with one careful hand. He kept his branch pressed tight against his body, and he peered out at the river.

The girls were laughing beside the water. They moved among the washing pools and lifted the clothes from the stones. Their voices rang out bright and clear over the waves.

He watched them fold the cloth and load it into the waggon. Their game made his heart feel lighter than it had felt for many days. Perhaps these people were kind after all.

Then one girl stood very still. She did not run with the others. She looked straight toward the place where he was hiding.

Ulysses held his breath. The leaves rustled softly in the wind, and nothing else moved on the shore.

At last he understood that he could not stay hidden forever. He was tired, hungry, and far from home, and he needed help. It was time to step out into the open and be seen.

He drew his leafy branch close around his body. Then he rose slowly from the thicket and walked toward the shore.

Ulysses lay still for a long moment, listening. The voices rose and fell, bright and clear above the sound of the water. He wanted to know more before he showed himself.

He pushed aside the bush and crept down toward the shore. He kept low, moving from rock to rock. Tall reeds hid him from view, and he went slowly, with great care.

Through the gaps in the reeds he saw the washing pools. Linen lay spread out across the warm stones to dry. Among the girls stood one who was taller than the rest. Her voice was clear and sweet, and it carried over the water like a song.

Ulysses remembered something his mother had taught him long ago. Strangers must always be treated kindly, and travellers deserve respect. He would not frighten these people with noise or sudden movement.

So he moved closer, one careful step at a time. He stepped over the dry sticks on the ground and did not snap a single twig. His heart beat fast, but his hands stayed steady.

At last he reached the edge of the open sand. Beyond it the girls laughed and splashed, their work spread around them. In a moment, they would look up and see him standing there.

He pulled the leafy branch tighter around his waist and waited.

He had come this far, and he would not turn back now.

Ulysses saw how brave she was. He saw too how frightened the others had become, and he knew he was a stranger in this land. He had no friends here, and no one to speak for him.

Above the river, the sun glittered on the moving water. The birds that had been singing in the olive trees had gone quiet. Ulysses noticed this and thought it strange. Something had frightened them, or perhaps someone was near.

Feeling steadier, he parted the leaves with one hand. Through the gap he could see the shore. Several young women stood by the washing pools, still folding linen and laying it in the wagon.

He listened to their voices with care. They sounded calm, not afraid. Ulysses weighed each word, as he had done in many dangerous places before.

He would not rush out with harsh words. He would speak softly and choose his phrases with care. Whoever these people were, he would be ready to speak to them when the moment came.

He parted the leaves with care. Then he looked at the trees around him and thought hard about the way down. A bad step could snap a branch, and a snapped branch could send the girls running before he had a chance to speak.

So he chose the path slowly. He moved from trunk to trunk, keeping low. Each time he stopped, he listened for a long moment. Only the splash of the river and the calls of the girls reached him.

His body ached. The salt sea had cut his skin, and his legs shook under him. He had been swimming for two days, and he was tired to his bones. Still, he pressed on, one careful step at a time.

At last the trees thinned, and he could see the shore. A tall girl stood on the sand, alone and calm. She did not look afraid. She stood straight, facing the water, as if the strange sea had no power over her.

Ulysses stopped in the shadow of an old tree. He watched her for a while. He weighed his words in his mind, one by one, and thought about how best to approach her.

We sat down by the cave wall and waited for the owner to come home. The cheeses were piled high around us, and the smell of fresh milk filled the air.

My men were restless. Eurylochus leaned close to me and whispered that we should take what we could and run. I shook my head and told them to wait.

I reminded them that the gods watch over guests and strangers. A kind host is a gift from Zeus, and we had come here hoping for kindness. We would show respect, even while we waited.

We lit a small fire at the back of the cave. We took a little cheese and offered it to the gods as a sacrifice, and we prayed quietly for safe passage. Then we ate some of the cheese ourselves.

After that, we sat in silence. Every sound made us jump. The wind moaned at the cave mouth, and far away we heard the bleating of sheep.

At last the flocks came slowly up the hill. We crept to the far end of the cave, pressing close together in the shadows. My heart beat so hard that I could hear it in my ears.

Then the owner’s heavy steps came closer, and we held our breath and watched the entrance.

We did not wait long inside. The cheeses were tempting, but I wanted to see the owner first. So I took a small group of men out into the open air.

The meadows near the shore were green and bright with sunshine. Tall grass moved softly in the breeze. We could smell the salt of the sea on the wind.

Not far away we saw wild goats grazing on the slopes. They lifted their heads to watch us, then went back to their eating. My men laughed quietly and said they had never seen such easy hunting. I told them to leave the goats alone for now.

We walked along the shore and talked about our long voyage. Some of the men sat down on the warm sand and rested their tired legs. For a short while, it felt like a peaceful holiday.

Then the sky began to darken. A grey cloud slid over the sun. From the hills we heard the flocks bleating, and the sound grew louder as the animals came closer to their pens.

I called my men together and we hurried back toward the cave. Our feet pounded over the stony ground. We slipped through the entrance just before the sound of heavy footsteps reached our ears.

We crouched in the shadows, hearts beating fast. The shepherd would soon come home, and we did not yet know what kind of man he was.

We waited in silence, watching the mouth of the cave and listening.

prompt: The cave is full of cheeses and lambs, and its owner is still away. What should Ulysses do while they wait?

He then tells the men to keep their voices low and wait. As the sun sinks, the flocks come up the hill, and the scene picks up as the shepherd comes into the cave.

Ulysses looked around the cave and felt uneasy. His men were hungry, and the cheeses were everywhere, but he did not want to take what was not theirs. Taking food from a stranger’s home seemed to him a poor way to begin a visit.

“We will leave something in return,” he said quietly. “A host who finds guests have helped themselves will not be pleased with us.”

He chose a round cheese from the nearest rack. He set it on a flat stone close to the entrance, where the owner would see it first. It was a small gift, but it showed that they had been there and meant no harm.

His men muttered among themselves. Some of them wanted to load the ship with lambs and kids at once. Ulysses held up his hand and asked them to keep their voices low. “We will wait,” he said. “Let the owner come to us. Then we will see what sort of man he is.”

They sat in the shadows near the wall and waited. Outside, the light began to fade over the hills. Ulysses watched the entrance and listened to the sea below. He told himself to stay calm and to think before he spoke.

At last came the sound of bleating and the soft beat of many feet. The flocks were climbing the hill toward the cave. Ulysses drew a slow breath and kept his eyes on the opening, ready for whatever would come through it.

The shepherd was near now, and the light from the doorway was dimming behind him.
